slides.title: The Engine of Deep Learning 🚂
slides.content:
# The Calculus of Backpropagation

Popularized in 1986 by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, **Backpropagation** is an efficient application of the calculus **Chain Rule** to compute gradients of the loss $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to every weight $w_{ij}$ in the network.

### The Chain Rule Decomposition:
For an output weight $w$ connecting hidden activation $a$ to output $z$ and loss $\mathcal{L}$:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}$$

| Chain Rule Component | Interpretation | Mathematical Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a}$ | Upstream gradient flowing back from subsequent layer | Error signal propagated backwards |
| $\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}$ | Local derivative of the activation function | Modulates flow (e.g. ReLU passes 1 if $z>0$, 0 if $z\le0$) |
| $\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}$ | Local derivative of linear pre-activation | Equals the incoming activation value $a_{\text{in}}$ |
| $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w}$ | Final partial derivative for parameter update | Fed to the optimizer to adjust weight: $w \leftarrow w - \alpha \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w}$ |

quizData.question: What mathematical principle enables backpropagation to compute gradients through dozens of composite network layers efficiently?
quizData.explanation: Backpropagation recursively applies the Chain Rule backwards from loss to inputs, caching intermediate derivatives to avoid duplicate computation.

slides.title: PyTorch Autograd in Action 🐍
slides.content: Witnessing automated computational graph backpropagation in PyTorch:
slides.codeSnippet:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)

# Forward pass: y = w * x + b; loss = (y - 10)^2
y = w * x + b      # 2*3 + 1 = 7.0
loss = (y - 10)**2 # (7 - 10)^2 = 9.0

# Backward pass
loss.backward()

print('dL/dw (analytic: 2*(y-10)*x = 2*(-3)*3 = -18):', w.grad.item())
print('dL/db (analytic: 2*(y-10)*1 = 2*(-3) = -6):', b.grad.item())

slides.title: AI Pro Tip: Computational Graphs 💡
slides.content:
## Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation
PyTorch builds a **Dynamic Computational Graph (DAG)** during the forward pass. Every operation records its input nodes and local derivative function.

When `loss.backward()` is called, the graph is traversed in topological reverse order, executing vector-Jacobian products in $O(1)$ passes regardless of the number of parameters!
